document_check.note: Mo W et al., Psychiatry Research 339 (2024) 116067, 'Prevalence of sleep disturbances in people with mild cognitive impairment: A systematic review and meta-analysis'. Subgroup analysis by geographical region is on p.12 and in Table 3 (p.13).

cited_result: Subgroup analysis of pooled subjective sleep-disturbance prevalence by geographical region: 'differed significantly (df = 3, Q = 34.025, p < 0.001)', North America 19.1%, Europe 40.9%, Asia 39.4%, Oceania 45.2% (p.12). Set against measurement method, 'df = 2, Q = 30.173, p < 0.001' (p.12).
tool_reason: The cited result is a subgroup (moderator) finding from a systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence studies, so ROBIS applies.

domains.rationale: The protocol was registered and published. Eligibility criteria and the definition of sleep disturbance are stated. The design restrictions (no case-control studies, no MMSE-only diagnosis) are justified, and there were no date or language restrictions.

signalling.question: 1.1 Did the review adhere to pre-defined objectives and eligibility criteria?
signalling.quote: We registered our review protocol with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD42022366108). This review was also conducted in accordance with a published protocol (Mo et al., 2023).

signalling.question: 1.2 Were the eligibility criteria appropriate for the review question?
signalling.quote: Studies were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: (1) included individuals with MCI as the primary study group; (2) reported sleep disturbances using a validated instrument

signalling.question: 1.3 Were eligibility criteria unambiguous?
signalling.quote: In the present study, sleep disturbances include long and short sleep duration, poor sleep quality, decreased SE, difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, early awakenings, increased number and length of awakenings, and excessive daytime sleepiness.

signalling.question: 1.4 Were all restrictions in eligibility criteria based on study characteristics appropriate?
signalling.quote: We did not include case–control studies because they cannot provide any information about the prevalence or incidence of a disease

signalling.question: 1.5 Were any restrictions in eligibility criteria based on sources of information appropriate?
signalling.quote: searched from inception to January 20, 2024, with no restriction on the publication date or language

domains.domain: Domain 2: Identification and selection of studies
domains.rationale: Six databases were searched with a librarian, supplemented by hand-searching reference lists and contacting authors. There were no language restrictions, and screening was done by two reviewers independently.

signalling.question: 2.1 Did the search include an appropriate range of databases/electronic sources for published and unpublished reports?
signalling.quote: the MEDLINE (Ovid), Embase (Elsevier), Cochrane Library ..., Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (EBSCOhost), PsycINFO (EBSCOhost), and Web of Science (Clarivate) databases were searched

signalling.question: 2.2 Were methods additional to database searching used to identify relevant reports?
signalling.quote: The reference lists of all included full-text articles were hand-searched to identify any additional relevant studies ... Some authors were contacted by email or ResearchGate

signalling.question: 2.3 Were the terms and structure of the search strategy likely to retrieve as many eligible studies as possible?
signalling.quote: In collaboration with an experienced librarian ... The full search strategy is detailed in the supplementary materials.

signalling.question: 2.4 Were restrictions based on date, publication format, or language appropriate?
signalling.quote: We translated non-English articles to determine their eligibility.

signalling.question: 2.5 Were efforts made to minimise error in selection of studies?
signalling.quote: Titles and abstracts were assessed by two independent reviewers (M.W and L.X) against the inclusion criteria

domains.domain: Domain 3: Data collection and study appraisal
domains.rationale: Extraction and JBI appraisal were each done by two reviewers independently. However, no rule is given for choosing among multiple prevalence estimates per study, and the case thresholds for the subjective instruments are not reported. Some objective 'prevalences' use thresholds derived from the sample mean or median. Quality was also reduced to a summed score used as an inclusion cut.

signalling.question: 3.1 Were efforts made to minimise error in data collection?
signalling.quote: Two independent reviewers (M.W and L.X) extracted data from the studies included in the review using the standardized JBI data extraction tool

signalling.question: 3.2 Were sufficient study characteristics available for both review authors and readers to be able to interpret the results?
signalling.quote: Table 1 Characteristics of the included studies (country, sample size, design, setting, MCI criteria, tool, tool type, prevalence); case thresholds for subjective tools not given

signalling.question: 3.3 Were all relevant study results collected for use in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: pMCI, 46.6 % (151); DSM-5, 46.0 % (70) [Lopez-Anton]; TST > 450 min, 25 % (16); TST < 360 min, 27.3 % (17) [Basta]; WASO > median, 45.95 % (17) [Menon]. (Searched for a rule for choosing among multiple estimates: none.)

signalling.question: 3.4 Was risk of bias (or methodological quality) formally assessed using appropriate criteria?
signalling.quote: The positive responses were summed, with the maximum score being 9 points ... Data synthesis was performed only for studies of fair (overall score, 4–6) and good (overall score, 7–9) methodological quality.

signalling.question: 3.5 Were efforts made to minimise error in risk of bias assessment?
signalling.quote: Two independent reviewers (M.W and L.X) critically appraised eligible studies for methodological quality using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist

domains.rationale: One 'subjective prevalence' pools constructs that are not equivalent, including self-report, informant NPI items, depression scales and a COVID questionnaire, with I2 = 98%. The region subgroup is a univariable comparison with 89-98% heterogeneity within subgroups. It is confounded with measurement method: all eight North American studies in the synthesis used informant scales (Table 1). No multivariable meta-regression or robustness check was done for the subgroup, and region is not among the pre-stated review questions.

signalling.question: 4.1 Did the synthesis include all studies that it should?
signalling.quote: Because only one study each was conducted in Africa and South America, and only one straddled multiple continents, meta-analysis of these studies was not possible

signalling.question: 4.2 Were all pre-defined analyses reported or departures explained?
signalling.quote: i) What is the sleep disturbance prevalence in MCI in clinic-based and community-based studies? ii) What is the sleep disturbance prevalence in MCI according to subjective and objective measures? (Region not among the stated questions; searched for pre-specified or a priori subgroups: none.)

signalling.question: 4.3 Was the synthesis appropriate given the nature and similarity in the research questions, study designs and outcomes across included studies?
signalling.quote: Subjective tools used for measuring sleep disturbances were primarily self-report scales [PSQI ..., Patient Health Questionnaire ..., “Conditions of Personal satisfaction during COVID-19 pandemic quarantine” questionnaire ...], informant rating scales [NPI ...], and clinician-administered instruments (... Hamilton Depression Rating Scale ...)

signalling.question: 4.4 Was between-study variation (heterogeneity) minimal or addressed in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: Finally, significant heterogeneity among studies remained even in subgroup analyses (Table 3: Asia I2 98.31, Europe 97.36, North America 89.42)

signalling.question: 4.5 Were the findings robust, e.g. as demonstrated through funnel plot or sensitivity analyses?
signalling.quote: Egger’s regression test revealed significant publication bias (t = 5.23, p < 0.001). According to Duval and Tweedie’s trim-and-fill method ... there was no significant variation in the adjusted effect sizes (leave-one-out applied to the overall estimate only)

signalling.question: 4.6 Were biases in primary studies minimal or addressed in the synthesis?
signalling.quote: we examined the effects of publication year, participant age, percentage of females, and study quality; none of these covariates significantly moderated the estimated sleep disturbance prevalence

domains.domain: Phase 3: Risk of bias in the review
domains.rationale: The authors attribute regional differences to sociocultural factors and sleep-medicine policy without addressing the fact that region and measurement method coincide. Their conclusion credits data source with contributing to heterogeneity despite a non-significant test (p = 0.395).

signalling.question: A. Did the interpretation of findings address all of the concerns identified in Domains 1 to 4?
signalling.quote: North America prioritizes sleep medicine, with robust government support, strict professional guidelines, and extensive research and education initiatives likely explaining why it had the lowest prevalence of sleep disturbances.

signalling.question: B. Was the relevance of identified studies to the review's research question appropriately considered?
signalling.quote: it is important to acknowledge that the lack of equivalence across studies in the sleep measurement instruments used hampers our ability to draw conclusions regarding the global prevalence

signalling.question: C. Did the reviewers avoid emphasising results on the basis of their statistical significance?
signalling.quote: Moreover, variations in the data source and sleep disturbance assessment method contributed to the notable heterogeneity

overall_rationale: Searching, selection and appraisal were sound. The synthesis behind the cited region moderator is not: non-equivalent instruments are pooled with I2 near 98%, and the region comparison is univariable, possibly not pre-specified, and confounded with measurement method. The interpretation does not address this confounding.

applicability.concern: Region is not separable from measurement method in this data set
applicability.rationale: All eight synthesised North American studies used informant scales (NPI-12, NPI-Q), and the informant-rated pooled prevalence (23.7%) is close to the North American estimate (19.1%).
